title: Verstappen and Lawson get grid drops after ‘clumsy’ clash
excerpt:
Red Bull’s Max Verstappen and Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson have been given grid penalties by the stewards following their “unacceptable” and “clumsy” incident during second practice in Mexico.

The pair – having missed FP1 as rookies Ayumu Iwasa and Nikola Tsolov took over their cars – crossed paths in the early stages of FP2 when Verstappen made a move on Lawson into Turn 12.

Lawson tried to get back ahead at the following left-hand turn through the stadium section, with Verstappen bouncing over the kerb on the exit and rejoining alongside the New Zealander, causing damage to the Red Bull’s floor and Racing Bulls’ front wing.

A red flag was thrown to recover the debris, and both drivers picked up their practice programmes – Verstappen finishing P5 and Lawson P9.

After the session, the stewards reviewed video footage and data, as well as speaking to Verstappen and Lawson, before issuing individual one-place grid drops.

“On the approach to Turn 12, Car 3 [Verstappen] was on a preparation lap and Car 30 [Lawson] was on a cool down lap preparing for another push lap,” read the stewards’ decision document. “The drivers of both cars behaved in a manner that was considered unacceptable by the stewards particularly in view of the warning that had been given at the Team Managers meeting earlier this day.

“Both drivers admitted the moves were unnecessary and ‘clumsy’.

“Noting that there had been similar incidents this year of actions between drivers in Free Practice, the stewards have decided to escalate the penalty from that of a formal warning to a grid position penalty particularly in view of the warning that had been provided at the Team Managers meeting and consistent with other incidents involving contact between the cars in Free Practice in previous years.”

Speaking after FP2, Racing Bulls team boss Alan Permane had also used the word “unnecessary” to describe Verstappen and Lawson’s coming together.

“I think one word, just ‘unnecessary’ in a practice session; completely unnecessary, and I say that to both of them,” commented Permane, after Verstappen criticised Lawson for “not very smart behaviour”.

"I don’t know what Max has said, I haven’t heard anything, but I’m sure he’s got his opinion and I’m sure Liam has got his opinion. Mine is it’s just not needed, and they can both do better.”

Verstappen and Lawson were also given a penalty point apiece by the stewards.

title: What the teams said – Friday in Mexico City
excerpt:
The drivers and teams report back on all the action from Friday practice at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez ahead of the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix.

Oct 31, 2026 2:37am UTC

Ferrari

Ferrari were the only team to run both full time drivers in FP1, and both had a decent session, looking quick on the hard and soft tyres. Charles Leclerc topped FP1 by a reasonable margin, with Lewis Hamilton a few places back after running a touch wide on his flying lap. Leclerc picked up where he left off in FP2, again going quickest despite locking up on his soft tyres and running wide at Turn 1 on his first attempt at a flying lap.

But Hamilton’s second session was not so smooth, as he was forced to park up trackside with a PU issue.

Charles Leclerc - FP1: 1:18.128, P1; FP2: 1:17.827, P1

"Overall, our performance looks quite alright but we still need to work on some of our limiting factors. It was quite tricky on track today, as the surface was slippery, so we will work on that to find some improvements for tomorrow."

Lewis Hamilton - FP1: 1:18.866, P4; FP2: 1:18.512, P11

"It wasn’t the most straightforward day for me, as I missed some running in FP1 and then had to stop early in FP2. Despite that, the car felt quick, so it was unfortunate that we had to stop before completing the long run. From a setup point of view, I don’t think we need to make too many changes, as the car is working well. We’ll investigate the issue tonight and do our best to be ready for tomorrow. I’m ready to make the most of what we have."

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Lewis Hamilton of Great Britain and Scuderia Ferrari sits behind a marshal on a moped to return to the pit lane during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Manuel Velasquez - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

McLaren

Leonardo Fornaroli had an eventful session for McLaren when he took over Norris’ cockpit. He locked up more than once, went for a spot of lawn mowing and sounded a little confused on the radio, but by and large he kept the car in one piece. As for Oscar Piastri, he had a quiet opener and finished inside the top 10. Roll on FP2, and Lando Norris looked strong, pushing Leclerc and winding up just a tenth off the Ferrari man. That was despite a big lock-up on the mediums for the World Champion, rendering that compound useless for the long runs. Piastri struggled by comparison, but he did catch one big slide that had the crowd on the edge of their seats.

Lando Norris - FP2: 1:17930, P2

"Not a bad day on the timesheets at the end of Free Practice 2, but the car is still proving a challenge to drive. The pace is definitely there but the field is incredibly tight at the minute, so it will come down to execution in tomorrow’s Qualifying. Thank you to Leo for his support Free Practice 1, we’ve still got plenty to work on overnight as a team, but the foundations are definitely there for us to build on."

Oscar Piastri - FP1: 1:19.376, P8; FP2: 1:18.469, P10

"Mexico is always a challenge with the altitude, low downforce and very little grip, but today felt slightly better than I expected. Even with a scruffy lap on the Softs in Free Practice 2, the underlying pace looks competitive, and the track was improving quickly as we went. We learned a lot across the sessions and if I tidy up the areas on my lap I need to, I’m confident we can be further up the order tomorrow."

Leonardo Fornaroli - FP1: 1:20.235, P17

"It was really exciting to be back on track in FP1 with McLaren Mastercard, and I’m grateful to the team and to Lando for giving me the chance to drive the MCL40. It was my first time on this circuit, and it wasn’t easy to find the confidence straight away to get the front tyres up to the right temperature on a track surface that, especially at the start, offered very little grip. In fact, a lock-up at Turn 1 ruined my first lap on the Softs.

"I’m really happy to be part of this team and to be working closely with the engineers, always trying to provide clear feedback to help develop the car to its full potential. It’s very important for me to keep gaining experience in Formula 1 as I develop as a driver: I’m already looking forward to getting back on track next Friday at Interlagos!"

Randy Singh, Senior Director, Racing

"All in all, it was a very productive Friday. We devoted a significant portion of our early practice sessions to set-up experiments and evaluations, particularly to adapt the car to the specific challenges of high altitude. Leo did a fantastic job of supporting our test programme in the opening session, providing us with a solid foundation on which to fine-tune performance in the afternoon. Both Lando and Oscar completed their planned programmes, using all three tyre compounds and running with different fuel loads on a track which, as is traditional here, offers little grip on the first day.

"Based on what we’ve seen today, the level of competitiveness is exceptionally close, with the top four teams separated by very small gaps and the rest of the field closer together than usual. Managing power unit and brake temperatures will be crucial for the rest of the weekend, especially in race conditions when running in traffic. We’ve seen numerous front-wheel lockups across the field, but we know where we can gain further lap times and feel well prepared to tackle qualifying and Sunday’s race."

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Lando Norris of Great Britain driving the (1) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Oscar Piastri of Australia and McLaren prepares to drive in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Leonardo Fornaroli of Italy driving the (67) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

Mercedes

Kimi Antonelli ran wide on one of his first laps out on track, but after that settled in and looked relatively quick in the opening session, as Fred Vesti kept him company in the top three in an accomplished showing. George Russell joined the fray in FP2, and went third fastest on his second push lap on the softs, showing he seems up for the fight here. That was a tenth faster than his team mate, with Mercedes having a very solid opening day in Mexico City.

Kimi Antonelli - FP1: 1:18.787, P2; FP2: 1:18.044, P4

"First of all, it was good to be back in the car and feeling healthy today. It was an interesting Friday here in Mexico; it's never easy to get a read on the car, particularly in FP1 when the track needs a lot of cleaning. We tried a few different things between the sessions to get the car balance in a better window, and it seems that we improved things for FP2.

"There are definitely more things we can improve going into tomorrow and we have some work to do overnight. Ferrari looked very quick, but we will focus on ourselves, see where we can find more performance and hopefully put ourselves in a good position for tomorrow."

George Russell - FP2: 1:17.933, P3

"Fred did a really good job in the car and set us up well for my hour of practice; it was good to get into a rhythm so quickly after sitting out FP1. Mexico is always a unique challenge because of the altitude and the low grip, and that feels even more pronounced this year. We've been running high levels of downforce at most circuits because of the way the cars operate on the straights, so coming here we don't have the same step up in downforce that we would normally have at this circuit. That makes the car particularly tricky to drive, and you also have the challenge of turbo lag at this altitude.

"It's incredibly tight out there and every bit of lap time is going to matter. Ferrari look the strongest at the moment, which is perhaps not a surprise given the characteristics of this circuit, but I think it could go any way by Q3 tomorrow. We need to maximise everything because the margins are going to be very small."

Fred Vesti - FP1: 1:18.861, P3

"My FP1 session today was really satisfying. We worked through our full programme, gained lots of valuable data both for this weekend and the longer term, and helped set up the rest of our day. Personally, I was also very happy with how I performed across the hour. I knew my soft tyre lap was a good one, but seeing P3 on the timing screens made me extremely happy. I've put a huge amount of work into this car with the team, going back to the start of its development two years ago, so to have the opportunity to drive it here in Mexico and put together a strong lap was very special.

"I'm very grateful for the trust the team has in me and for the opportunity to show what I can do. These sessions are important for all us rookies, so I am pleased to make the most of it today. I felt comfortable in the car, put together a good lap and was really pleased to finish P3. It was a great experience and one I really enjoyed."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"It's been a solid first day in Mexico. Kimi and Fred both did a good job in FP1, particularly given how difficult the conditions can be here with the altitude and low grip. Fred completed the programme we had planned for him and did an excellent job to finish P3. That gave us useful information to carry into FP2 when George returned to the car.

"Mexico is the hardest track to prepare for as it's impossible to simulate all the effects of altitude. We use Friday to understand the various issues that we are facing and come up with an approach to managing those through qualifying and the race.

"From the power unit side, we seem to be in reasonable shape with good delivery of power out of the corners. The cooling for both brakes and power unit is always an issue here but we were able to do decent long runs on both cars and whilst we'd like a bit more margin, it seems like all teams are having to do some management.

"The field is tight and we wouldn't put ourselves at the front of the bunch from today's running. We're struggling with a lack of stability on entry that moves to apex understeer. The single lap issues are actually quite similar to the long run, which should make it a bit easier to progress, but it's clear we need to find a step if we want to be challenging for the front row."

(Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: George Russell of Great Britain driving the (63) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Ryan Pierse/Getty Images)

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Frederik Vesti of Denmark driving the (72) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images)

Red Bull

Max Verstappen sat out the first session for Iwasa, who had a good hour for Red Bull. Isack Hadjar had a more difficult time of it, complaining about his steering wheel not being on straight, and also issues with the brakes. In the second session, Hadjar made his way up through the field with less to complain about. But his team mate did not have a smooth time of it, instead making contact with Lawson as the two jostled for position. That left the Dutchman with a heavily damaged floor, meaning he set his fastest lap time in a car that was definitely lacking in some downforce.

Max Verstappen - FP2: 1:18.138, P5

“Today was a tough session and we probably could have done a little bit better, but we weren’t too far off. It is a different kind of challenge here as the high altitude is always quite extreme. It is tricky with the grip and the sliding, but I think everyone else will be saying the same thing as it never feels great at this circuit. There is some fine tuning to do and we just need to find more pace in the car to make a real jump. We got a little bit of damage from the incident with Liam too. The Ferraris are looking quick in this session; this is a track where you need to have more low-speed performance so it should play into their strengths.”

Isack Hadjar - FP1: 1:19.545, P11; FP2: 1:18.237, P6

“FP1 was a tricky session for us with only a few push laps on the board, but we managed to sort the issue out quickly and get some long running at the end. We made some good set-up changes for FP2, which showed. I felt a lot more comfortable in the car and we were more competitive. There are a few things we need to tidy up, but the long run has seemed good so far. The day started a little rough for us but ended with some positives. I think we can be in the fight.”

Ayumu Iwasa - FP1: 1:19.113, P5

“It was great to be back out there. Going into an FP1 session, you don’t really care about the ranking or the lap time; you just need to focus on doing the job. It’s been a little while since I last drove the car at Monza, but I could really feel the differences since then. The car performed well in both low-speed and high-speed corners, which gave me the confidence to push to the limit. It also felt quick, which always makes it more fun to drive. We managed to get some clear feedback that we’ll take into the rest of the weekend, so it was a solid session for me.”

Pierre Wache, Technical Director

“Ayumu did a very good job in FP1, where we got plenty of testing done. On top of that, he showed impressive pace for a young driver. In FP2, the performance of Max’s car was clearly affected by some damage, which we will be able to fix for FP3, whereas Isack’s session was solid overall. Still, we have a lot of work to do. The long run was more or less there, but we have performance to find, as the drivers are not yet happy with the balance. We are confident we can improve that with the set-up for tomorrow."

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Ayumu Iwasa of Japan driving the (36) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Racing Bulls

Nikola Tsolov was making his FP1 debut for Racing Bulls, and as a result his times were some of the most eye-catching. He wound up just two places and one tenth behind his team mate, Lindblad just scraping into the top 10 ahead of him. Arvid Lindblad had another good session in the afternoon, again finishing in the top 10. Liam Lawson’s FP2 will be remembered for some wheel-to-wheel action with Verstappen though, the two former team mates both winding up with car damage after fighting over the same piece of tarmac.

Arvid Lindblad - FP1: 1:19.478, P10; FP2: 1:18.389, P7 Liam Lawson - FP2: 1:18.455, P9 Nikola Tsolov – FP1: 1:19.604, P12

Lindblad said

“Today was pretty decent overall. The altitude makes this circuit quite unique so FP1 was a little challenging, particularly as these are new conditions for the PU. The team made some good changes heading into FP2, and the car felt more alive. There are still a few things to work on ahead of tomorrow, but I think we’re in a good place. I really enjoy driving this track and I’m looking forward to the rest of the weekend. We’ll see what we can achieve in Qualifying tomorrow, but the target is definitely Q3.”

Tsolov said

“It was a super special day today and something I’ve dreamt of since I started racing. The atmosphere in F1 is very different, it’s crazy. I came into the session without putting too much pressure on myself and the team really helped me with that in making sure I felt the best I could, so I’m really grateful for that. The car is certainly different to what I’ve ever driven, it was tough to get used to but I got up to pace pretty quickly. I ticked all the boxes for what we needed to get out of the session and I’m looking forward to improving at every chance I get. I really enjoyed myself and I’m looking forward to spending the rest of the weekend with the team and learning as much as I can.”

Alan Permane, Team Principal said

“A strong day for us. The car has worked well across both sessions. Nikola did a great job for his first time in this car and at this track; the pace was there and he did everything we asked of him. We did a bit of aero testing with him and one of his objectives was to help with feedback and pick up differences in a couple of the specifications we ran, and he did that very well.

The car was in a decent window in FP2, the pace looks good on both long and short runs. Liam had an unfortunate and unnecessary incident with Max , which I think they both could have handled better. When you’re going for an out lap, it’s really important you do the last sector fast, which they were both going for.”

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Arvid Lindblad of Great Britain driving the (41) Visa Cash App Racing Bulls VCARB 03 RB Ford on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Nikola Tsolov of Bulgaria and Visa Cash App Racing Bulls and Peter Bayer, CEO of Visa Cash App Racing Bulls in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

Alpine

Pierre Gasly had a good opening session with a top six finish for Alpine, albeit with plenty of big name drivers sitting out. He was joined by Gabriele Mini, who was another making his FP1 debut. The Italian did well, although he did run over the grass at one point. In the second session, Gasly showed his FP1 result was no fluke with another strong lap to land solidly in the top 10. Franco Colapinto struggled to get up to speed after missing that first session, so he will be playing catch up tomorrow.

Pierre Gasly - FP1: 1:19.210, P6; FP2: 1:18.407, P8

“It has been a positively surprising Friday for us where we have had one of our better Practice days of the season so far. We arrived here expecting some challenges given the conditions and some uncertainties as to how the car would behave at this circuit. We have had two good sessions today where I have felt good right from the first laps of the day. The altitude here always makes the car feel strange but, compared to recent years at this track, I am feeling much more at ease. We have a good baseline to work from going into the rest of the weekend where we have a few areas to fine tune. It's not massive things which we need to improve, a bit on braking as well as getting the car more comfortable with some bumps in the high-speed, but it's quite small details. The gaps are also small, only a few hundredths between a few cars, and it will be about putting it all together when it counts.”

Franco Colapinto - FP2: 1:19.132, P16

“Even though it might not look that way from the lap times, the overall feeling after today was positive. We were catching up a little after missing Free Practice 1, but we are not as far off as maybe the timings show. I made a small error in the final sector and did not get the most out of my Soft tyre run. I know exactly where I need to improve for tomorrow and will also work with the team overnight to put ourselves in a stronger position. The long run pace was also positive, so if we can qualify well, we should hopefully be in contention for some points this weekend.”

Gabriele Mini - FP1: 1:19.946, P14

“That was an amazing experience for me to drive for the first time in an official Formula One session. Firstly, a big thank you to Flavio, Steve and the team for the opportunity, it was a truly memorable moment for me. As I left the garage, I was waiting in the pit lane with Lewis [Hamilton] in front of me, which was very cool. There were some legends of the sport out on track, people I have looked up to since I was a kid, so to be there with them was incredibly special. I would say the session itself was positive on our side. The team had a clear plan for me which meant some aero testing and data collection which will hopefully benefit the team in the future. I tried to stay consistent and build up the pace lap after lap. I did some good laps but if I am being critical of myself, I did not click everything together so that is something for me to look at and learn from. It's a very unique circuit with the conditions; tough on aero, tough on the power unit and there is a lot to understand and manage. That is all part of the learning process, though, and it was great to experience it all for the first time.”

Steve Nielsen, Managing Director

“Taking the day as a whole, I think we can be largely positive and confident heading into the rest of the weekend. We won't rest on our laurels though and we know we still have work to do and it's incredibly tight, particularly on one lap pace. Pierre really got into a good groove today and spoke very highly of his feeling inside the car, which is something we want to carry over into Qualifying tomorrow. Franco also fed back that he has a good feeling and knows where he can improve. The high fuel running in particular looked strong, but we know the field is more closely matched in Qualifying, so we need to look at extracting everything over a single lap. Also, it was a great job by Gabriele today, which was his first time in this car, and he did exactly what we expected of him.”

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Pierre Gasly of France driving the (10) Alpine F1 A526 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Franco Colapinto of Argentina driving the (43) Alpine F1 A526 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Mark Thompson/Getty Images)

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Gabriele Mini of Italy driving the (62) Alpine F1 A526 Mercedes on the grass during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images)

Haas

Ollie Bearman had an eventful end to his first session, pulling into the pits with a smoking car that initially looked to be caused by a brake fire. He was swift to jump out, but it turned out to be a PU issue and Haas needed to change that unit between sessions. Esteban Ocon had sat out the opening session, but he returned in FP2 and immediately complained about the power steering. He was not happy later on either, when he was told to switch to the mediums for his long run, not the softs. As for Bearman, his second session was also disrupted, as he briefly parked in a run-off area before getting going again. He wound up needing a software change to his car.

Esteban Ocon – FP2: 1:18.774, P13

“It’s always challenging when you miss out on a session, but Ryō did a good job and collected some valuable data. In FP2, we had a small issue at the start of the session, which we quickly fixed, and then it was about getting up to speed as quickly as we could. I still don’t feel super comfortable in the car, so there will be some adjustments to make and some work to be done overnight ahead of FP3 and Quali tomorrow.”

Oliver Bearman - FP1: 1:19.412, P9; FP2: 1:18.849, P14

“Overall, it’s been a positive day on track. We encountered a lot of issues in FP1, as we lost our latest spec engine, so we’re having to revert to the previous one which is a shame, as obviously there’s some performance involved in there. The car was a bit more tricky in FP2, so we need to understand why, but in general I’ve been happy with the day. I’m looking forward to tomorrow, I think things will be feeling better and I’m excited to see how it goes.”

Ryo Hirakawa - FP1: 1:19.982, P15

“First of all, a big thanks to the team. I’m really happy to feel the step in terms of performance since I drove in Budapest, so hats off to the team. We completed the run program, had no issues on the car, and we’ve made a step forward for FP2 with Esteban being back in the car. I’m really happy I had a good session, so hopefully we can score good points on Sunday.”

Ayao Komatsu, Team Principal

“We made a very good start. The car was competitive straight away, and both Ollie and Ryō looked very comfortable. It was good to hear from Ryō, as the last time he gave feedback was before our update, so he confirmed what our drivers have been saying about consistency, predictability, and stability of the package. Ollie was very happy, in low-speed he was mega, even in high-speed – which is one of our weaknesses – he was doing a very good job. Unfortunately, we had a PU issue, so Ollie’s FP1 was cut short at the end. The team did an unbelievable job between sessions to replace the engine and other damaged parts to send the car out on time. In FP2, Ollie was less happy with the car, operationally it was okay, but less of a clean session, if you like. Fundamentally, the car is still performing reasonably competitively, so we just need to clean up some areas overnight and prepare for FP3.”

Aston Martin

Jak Crawford did not have the best FP1, after he was told to park up trackside with an issue. That ended his running, Aston Martin later saying a suspected ERS problem had curtailed his session. Fernando Alonso though had a strong opener, finishing solidly in the top 10. The Spaniard impressed again in FP2, winding up 12th and showing the car does have some potential around this track.

Fernando Alonso - FP1: 1:19.357, P7; FP2: 1:18.596, P12

Lance Stroll - FP2: 1:19.631, P20

Jak Crawford - FP1: 1:20.803, P19

Alonso said:

"It has been a solid Friday in terms of performance here in Mexico, and we feel a little closer today than we have at previous events.

"It is always a challenging circuit, so it is encouraging to start the weekend on a positive note.

"The altitude brings its own difficulties, but we will keep working overnight and aim to get the most out of the car tomorrow and on Sunday."

Crawford said:

"It was a decent day for me despite an early end to the session. We had to stop the car on track due to a battery issue, but still managed to get some good running in today.

title: How 10 F1 rookies got on during FP1 in Mexico City
excerpt:
Traditionally, the Mexico City Grand Prix sees a rush of rookies participating in FP1, with several drivers on the current grid having made their first public F1 appearances at the track in previous seasons.

This year brought a bumper crop of 10 youngsters running in Friday's opening session, with only Ferrari fielding both of their race drivers.

The group included some familiar faces, several of whom have participated in FP1 sessions across multiple seasons. Inevitably, the focus was on the three making their first public appearance in a current F1 car – particularly one driver who remains a genuine contender for a 2027 race seat.

Tsolov takes his chance

Racing Bulls boss Alan Permane made it clear a few weeks ago that F2 star Nikola Tsolov is in the frame alongside Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad. Inevitably, that added another layer of intrigue to the Bulgarian's public debut.

However, speaking to F1 TV, Permane stressed that the day was not a shootout.

"I said to him look, this isn't an audition, this isn't a rehearsal or anything like that,” Permane noted. “We know he's got pace, we know he's fast – we see that in F2. And I said to him what we're looking for is your feedback. We want to hear what you've got to say about the car. We want to hear about what you've got to say about the changes we make to the car, and then we want to hear how you are in the debrief.”

Having already gained some mileage in TPC running at Imola, Tsolov enjoyed a clean session and finished P12, just 0.126s shy of Lindblad.

“I think I was ready for it,” Tsolov said. “To be honest, I didn't really think about it too much, didn't really stress it, so I managed to arrive in a calm mental state.

“I don't have any reference. So, for me, it's just what it is. They've done already 20 rounds, so they kind of maybe felt different to the other places with the altitude, but definitely all the electric part of the car and the engine was something that I really had to get used to, and it's something very new for me.

“So, I think I can do a lot better – just keep on building onto that and learning more about how everything works.”

For Tsolov's F2 rival Gabriele Mini, Friday marked a first appearance in the Alpine A526 after TPC running in July. The Italian finished P14, with a best lap 0.756s slower than team mate Pierre Gasly.

“Both the team and I are pretty happy about how everything went,” Mini said. “We got a bit unlucky with the VSC timing at the end, which really didn't allow us to do any push laps on soft, just one.”

If Audi are proven to be correct regarding Freddie Slater, his appearance will be remembered as the F1 debut of a future talent. Not only did the Briton only turn 18 in July, but he has also yet to race an F2 car, so this was quite a step for him.

His session was ultimately blighted by issues beyond his control, with an error in the garage seeing him leave the pit lane with a cooling fan still attached and blocking a radiator inlet – an incident that later earned Audi a €7,500 fine.

Slater only got a brief unrepresentative run at the end of the session and had to settle for P21 with a best time more than 1.3s off Nico Hulkenberg’s best. Given his youth, he remained remarkably philosophical about the experience.

FP1 REPORT: Leclerc leads Antonelli in Mexico City as new faces make F1 debuts

"At the end of the day, it's motorsport, and that's how things go,” the F3 runner up said. “We're a team, and we win as a team, and we lose as a team. So of course, it was a bit frustrating, obviously, not to get many laps.

“But overall, that one lap that I did do was actually pretty good compared to relevant data. And a historic day for Audi to have their first junior driver in the car. It's a very special day, so we look at the positives.”

The young Briton gets another chance to showcase his talents with another practice appearance scheduled for Sao Paulo next week.

Vesti impresses with third

Of those with previous FP1 experience, the standout performer was Fred Vesti, making his third outing for Mercedes in Mexico City after appearances in 2023 and 2025.

The Dane finished the session in P3, just 0.074s shy of World Champion-elect Kimi Antonelli.

Vesti may be operating somewhat under the radar given that he has no obvious path to an F1 race seat. However, after the session he made the surprise revelation that he is chasing one and thus Friday was "perfect timing." The Brackley team certainly knows his value.

“Every time he gets in the car and does an FP1, he steps it up a level,” said Deputy Team Principal Bradley Lord. “And that was his most convincing FP1 so far.

“I think you can see that he's a guy who, away from this paddock, is racing regularly, obviously an IMSA champion as well, and is able to step in and ready to race at any point. So, a really good job.”

The only rookie to outpace his team mate was Red Bull’s Ayamu Iwasa in P5, six places and 0.432s ahead of Isack Hadjar. The comparison was skewed by power unit issues that compromised the Frenchman's session, but nevertheless it was a solid performance from the Super Formula star.

Having missed out on a 2027 Haas race seat, Iwasa’s countryman Ryo Hirakawa also had a good session as he logged P15, 0.570s shy of Ollie Bearman.

Mixed fortunes for the rest

Mexico was a third FP1 outing of the year for McLaren’s Leonardo Fornaroli following Barcelona and Budapest. It was a frustrating session for the Italian as he ran off track more than once, flat spotting his soft tyres in the process. The 2023 F3 and 2024 F2 champion ultimately finished P17.

“Overall, it was a tricky session,” Fornaroli said. “Of course, it was a new track for me, and it wasn't easy to build confidence. It was very low grip, especially at the start of the session, and then putting temperature into the tyres was very hard as well.

“I had a front lock up straight away into T1 because I didn't manage to put the right temperature into the front tyres, and this, of course, compromised the whole soft run and performance in general.”

Jak Crawford enjoyed his fourth FP1 run of 2026 with Aston Martin and he appeared to have inherited Lance Stroll’s luck with unreliability when he stopped on track with an ERS issue after running just 15 laps. That left the American in P19, one spot ahead of Luke Browning, who was enjoying his third outing with Williams.

At the bottom of the times in P22 was Colton Herta in Valtteri Bottas' Cadillac, as the American continues his push towards securing the all-important Super Licence.

“I was under the impression coming in this weekend if I do this, I get the Super Licence,” Herta said. “So, I guess I have to wait and see. For me the biggest thing has been to not worry about that stuff and just drive the car.

“And so that's kind of what I've focused on all year, because it has been a discussion in my career for a lot of years now. And I just try to drive the car and do what I can do.”

title: Piastri on why McLaren’s Mexico prospects are ‘very difficult to know’
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri was left feeling that McLaren’s prospects going forward at the Mexico City Grand Prix are “difficult to know” after the opening day of action on Friday.

Piastri was joined in Free Practice 1 by the squad’s reserve driver Leonardo Fornaroli, with the Australian placing eighth on the timesheets ahead of the rookie in P17.

Lando Norris then returned to action later on in second practice and the Briton proved to be the closest challenger to pacesetter Charles Leclerc on the timesheets, ending the hour in P2 while Piastri placed in 10th.

It was an eventful Free Practice 2, with Piastri experiencing a close call with the barriers, but the 25-year-old felt that the day had been reasonable for McLaren.

“I think we looked okay, to be honest,” he explained after the second session. “Ferrari have looked very strong, I would say, but I think we look all right. My lap on the soft in FP2 was pretty scruffy at the end, but I think it’s going reasonably well.

“It’s always very tricky here in Mexico with the conditions, and I feel like the track’s improving quite quickly. But it felt like it was an okay day.”

Looking ahead to Saturday, Piastri was reluctant to draw too many conclusions about what the papaya squad might expect, particularly given the presence of numerous rookie drivers across many teams during Free Practice 1.

“It’s very difficult to know,” the nine-time race winner said. “I think especially on a day like today, where so many people missed FP1, it’s always a little bit tricky. But I feel like there’s plenty to learn and try to improve for tomorrow.”

Randy Singh, McLaren’s Senior Racing Director, gave a positive assessment of how Friday had gone for the team, particularly in terms of Fornaroli’s performance.

“The day was really good,” he summarised. “I want to thank Leo, he drove in FP1, we had a lot of tests, a lot of experiments on his car, to help put the car in the right spot for this event. Which is tricky with the high altitude.

“He did a really good job. We spent most of FP1 doing that, getting the car in a good spot, then in FP2, trying to dial the performance in a little bit more.

“Today was reasonable for us, but the top teams are the same and it's very tight at the front for the top four. I'd say the midfield looks a lot closer than it has been at recent races so Qualifying will be tight.

“This is a circuit where people are going to have issues managing temperatures on Sunday, so there's going to be some challenges that carry forward to Sunday.

"You saw a lot of lock-ups today and I think it will be the same on Sunday as well.”

title: Hamilton reflects on ‘really unfortunate’ Mexico FP2 stoppage
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has admitted that Ferrari are “still investigating” exactly what went wrong with his car in FP2 at the Mexico City Grand Prix, with the Briton “praying that everything’s okay”.

As the only team not to run a rookie during the first hour of practice, Ferrari put their challenger to the test in different ways, including fitting an aero rake to Hamilton’s SF-26 before he embarked on his representative laps.

He ultimately finished fourth behind leader Charles Leclerc and the Mercedes pair of Kimi Antonelli and Fred Vesti, but any hope of finding more time later in the day was disrupted when he was ordered to stop the car after suffering a power-related issue.

Asked how he felt before the stoppage, which restricted him to P11 on the timesheets, Hamilton said: “I was feeling really good in the car – it’s just my luck. I think we did a really good job in getting the set-up in a better place. Just really unfortunate.

“I think we’re really competitive this weekend as a team. I didn’t get to do the long runs so I have no idea, but I know it’s really hard to overtake here, as you saw with some people out there. They’re still investigating to find out what was wrong, and just praying that everything’s okay.

“I missed a little bit of time in FP1 because we did the rake running. Normally I would have one of the young drivers do FP1 at this track like most people did, but I opted to do it somewhere else.

“Basically I’ve only really had one session because I missed at least half of that session. I don’t think we need to make many changes to the set-up. I’d probably leave it much the same because we were very quick.

“I think I already had a loss of power earlier on in the lap and was still quick. I’ll give it everything tomorrow and just try to do the best with whatever I have.”

Team Principal Fred Vasseur explained on Friday that the team will “take a decision tonight” on what needs to be done to fix Hamilton’s car before FP3 and Qualifying, but was satisfied overall with Ferrari’s showing.

Although Leclerc topped both sessions, his advantage reduced from nearly seven-tenths to 0.103s, leaving the team acutely aware of the close competition at Mexico City’s unique circuit.

“It's very early stages,” Vasseur said. “You know that Mexico is a challenge – it is a challenge with the altitude and for the car, for the drivers to find the limit.

“It is like it is – it's the same for everybody and we have to do a lot of work tonight to improve the situation.

“The pace was there from this morning. From the first lap the pace was there on the long stint, on one lap, and it means that we have to finetune. We still have a lot of work to do on the set-up and on the car because it's quite extreme conditions.

“You know that each weekend the competition is mega tight. Last year you had half a tenth between P2 and P6 and you can move from hero to zero. Let's be focused on ourselves, don't think about classification and try to do the best from what we have.”

title: Verstappen reacts to Lawson FP2 incident in Mexico
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has claimed that the incident with Liam Lawson during Free Practice 2 ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix was a result of "not very smart behaviour".

Both Verstappen and Lawson were looking to make up for lost time in the second, one-hour session on Friday having missed FP1, with their seats taken by Formula 1 young drivers Ayumu Iwasa and Nikola Tsolov respectively.

The pair crossed paths during the early proceedings of FP2 when Verstappen went for an overtake on the Racing Bulls driver ahead into Turn 12.

Lawson then attempted to re-pass into the following left turn through the stadium section, with Verstappen bouncing over the kerb on the exit and rejoining alongside the New Zealander, damaging his Red Bull's floor in the process.

A red flag was briefly deployed to recover the debris as both drivers continued until the end of the session, with Verstappen P5 and Lawson P9.

"I don't think it's called unlucky," said Verstappen when asked if it was just an unfortunate coming together.

"Maybe not very smart behaviour what he was trying to do there. At the end of the day, it's not going to change my weekend but if I would be him, I would act a little bit smarter. Also when you're fighting for your seat, it's not very smart behaviour."

Racing Bulls have yet to confirm their line-up for the 2027 season, with Tsolov making his F1 debut this weekend in FP1, finishing just one-tenth slower than Arvid Lindblad and in possible contention for Lawson's seat.

The incident between Verstappen and Lawson will be investigated post-session by the stewards, with Racing Bulls Team Principal Alan Permane critical of both drivers.

"I think one word, just 'unnecessary' in a practice session. Completely unnecessary and I say that to both of them," he said.

"I don't know what Max has said, I haven't heard anything, but I'm sure he's got his opinion and I'm sure Liam has got his opinion but mine is, it's just not needed and they can both do better."

title: Competitive order ‘can go any way’ in Mexico City – Russell
excerpt:
George Russell shared his confidence that the close competition shown during Friday’s running in Mexico City proved that Qualifying “can go any way”, with the Briton hoping to “pull the lap out when it matters”.

Many teams, including Mercedes, opted to field a rookie in the first hour of practice, which meant that Russell temporarily gave up his seat for reserve driver Fred Vesti.

That put him on the back foot in terms of track time, but he quickly caught up and finished third in FP2 with a time of 1m 17.933s – just 0.003s slower than McLaren’s Lando Norris, and around a tenth adrift of pace-setter Charles Leclerc.

“Always coming to Mexico, [there are] challenges with the altitude,” Russell reflected. “I think one big difference this year is that the majority of teams have been running high downforce at all of the tracks because we’ve got the SM that opens on the rear and the front on all of the straights.

“What that means is usually when we come to Mexico, we go to our maximum downforce from medium or low downforce, whereas this year we’ve always been on our maximum downforce.

“Coming to Mexico, it’s even lower grip than we’re used to. Turbo lag is an issue but it’s very tight out there between the top four teams.

“It’s fair to say Ferrari are looking strongest at the moment. Leclerc didn’t properly finish his lap, I don’t think, and Lewis [Hamilton] had the issue.

“We expected on this sort of circuit for them to perform best – they’ve got a very good chassis – but come Q3, I think it can go any way. As it stands, it can go any way so I need to pull the lap out when it matters.”

Mercedes Deputy Team Principal Bradley Lord echoed Russell’s comments about the unique nature of the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, but similarly anticipated that they have the “potential” to be in the battle for pole position.

“A solid day for us, I’d say – not spectacular, but solid,” Lord explained. “There are a lot of challenges here with PU cooling, with brake cooling, with boost management with these turbos now that we don’t have an MGU-H to help us out with that as we have done for the last few years.

“This is a tricky place to get everything right, to be quick on a single lap but also be able to maintain your pace for the long runs. We’ve answered a few of those questions. We’ve got a bit more digging to do through the data to find exactly the best compromise for tomorrow and Sunday.

“We’re always aiming to be up there fighting for pole, fighting for the front row and the front couple of rows. It looks like we’ve got the potential to do that, and now we’ve got to take the right steps to make sure we can deliver on that potential tomorrow.”

During Friday's teams' press conference in Mexico, Haas Team Principal Komatsu stated that he was unable to go into the details about the contract extension delay, but that "it's very clear from both parties, from Ollie's side, we want to continue working together".

When asked if Bearman was requesting an excessive salary increase, with rumours circulating of 6 million euros, Komatsu blasted the suggestion.

"I have no idea where that came from. Honestly, I've experienced it sometimes this season as well. People say there is no smoke without fire, but some people really invent a story," he said.

"What happened in Miami about apparently I had an argument with Esteban [Ocon], there's just absolutely zero truth in it and even those people claiming that they have some insider information etc, absolute total nonsense. This one, again I don't know who smoked up this 6 million euro number, that's the first time I saw it on Instagram.

"Someone came up, this is a good thing to stir whatever up. I have no comments to make because it's just not even close to the truth. Why do we engage in such absolute nonsense, what's the point of it?

"Those people creating are not trying to help anything. It's amazing these days that people don't check the source. I want to get more clicks, get more likes, so they cut and paste those stories and keep running with it, and before you know it, there are 20 people running the story and they think it's the truth. It's absolute nonsense."

If Bearman is retained it will mean that two Ferrari junior drivers will be driving for Haas next year, with current Formula 2 championship leader Rafael Camara having been confirmed as replacing Esteban Ocon in 2027.

With Haas using Ferrari's engines and other car components, suggestions were made to Komatsu that the partnership was similar to that between Red Bull and Racing Bulls, something he denied.

"I think the way Red Bull and Racing Bulls are set up is very different to how we collaborate with Ferrari. We don't have the same owner," he said.

"We are two completely independent teams and then we don't have a global programme in terms of how we bring the driver together, whereas Racing Bulls and Red Bull clearly work together, right? So that is a very different dynamic.

"Our collaboration with Ferrari, what it gives us, is access and opportunities. With Ollie for the first time here in FP1. That opportunity was available via our collaboration with Ferrari.

"But at no point did Ferrari say, 'Oh, can you take Ollie as your race driver?' Same as Rafael Camara.

"Of course, looking at the junior series, he's shown incredible speed and exciting talent. And then, because of our collaboration, we had access.

"We developed talks and we said, 'Okay, can we test Rafa in a TPC?' We all agreed, we tested, and he was very, very fast. So, we chose him. Again, I have no concern. It's just a benefit of our collaboration with Ferrari that we have access to those youngsters."

title: Leclerc tops eventful FP2 from Norris at Mexico City GP
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc ended Friday’s running at the Mexico City Grand Prix as the quickest driver on track as he beat Lando Norris and George Russell to the top of the timesheets in FP2.

10 drivers had vacated their seats for the first hour of practice to give rookies a chance to run, so nearly half the grid had track time to recover. It was no surprise, then, that a long queue of cars had formed at the end of the pit lane by the point the light turned green at 1600 local time.

One of the first to venture out was Haas’ Esteban Ocon, who reported that he had “no power steering” on his installation laps, forcing him to head back to the garage just as team mate Ollie Bearman momentarily pulled to the side of the track.

While the Briton was able to get going again and join his team mate in the pits, Max Verstappen set an early benchmark of 1m 20.474s on a set of soft tyres, which was quickly eclipsed by Arvid Lindblad and Isack Hadjar.

Once the opening efforts were complete for most – with the notable exception of Leclerc, who only just held onto his car following a scary snap – Lewis Hamilton led for Ferrari, having posted a 1m 18.741s.

However, Leclerc’s first representative time was enough to edge out Hamilton by nearly five-tenths as he avoided being caught out by lock-ups that drivers up and down the grid, including McLaren’s Norris, continued to suffer.

Lawson insisted that the Red Bull racer “literally drove into me” as the incident was noted by the stewards, Verstappen returning to action with just under 40 minutes to go.

Focus shifted back towards cutting down lap times, with Norris successfully doing so as he surged into first place for McLaren, demoting Leclerc to P2 whilst wide moments and a big lock-up affected the Monegasque’s laps on the soft compound.

Unfortunately for Ferrari, their struggles continued in the form of an issue for Hamilton, who was ordered to stop the car on track. A Virtual Safety Car was deployed before an earlier radio message revealed that he said: “Something’s wrong with the power. I lost all power from Turn 13.”

Leclerc offered the Italian squad some hope as he reclaimed P1 with a 1m 17.827s, denying Norris and standings leader Kimi Antonelli prior to Russell’s improvement to P3, where he found himself only 0.003s adrift of the McLaren driver’s attempt.

Hamilton marginally missed out after his early end to the session and was followed by Fernando Alonso, the Haas pair of Ocon and Bearman, and Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg.

Franco Colapinto claimed P16 from Sainz, Sergio Perez (Cadillac), Alex Albon (Williams), Lance Stroll (Aston Martin), Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac) and Gabriel Bortoleto, the last of whom eventually made it out on track after Audi amended a technical issue.

title: Ferrari call for track changes at 'almost dangerous' Mexico City GP
excerpt:
Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur called for track changes to be made overnight at the Mexico City Grand Prix, arguing that some of the bumps are "almost dangerous" at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

Despite an afternoon of mixed fortunes for the Scuderia, with Charles Leclerc topping both FP1 and FP2 and Lewis Hamilton's SF-26 grinding to a halt in the second hour of running, Vasseur was more concerned with the condition of the circuit.

He highlighted how some of the bumps proved treacherous, and advocated remedial work before FP3, which is not uncommon in F1.

Issues with track surfaces do crop up, and venues are usually receptive to making changes and quick to implement them.

Reflecting on the opening two sessions of the weekend, Vasseur was keen to downplay the pace seen from Leclerc, dismissing the idea that the Italian team should carry any confidence into the second day of running.

"I don't have to be confident or not. We have to work. We have to try to get the best for [FP3 and qualifying]," Vasseur said after FP2. "Conditions are mega extreme. That we knew before with the altitude; it's a challenge.

"It's a challenge for us, but also for the others. It means that we have a lot of work to do... and it's mega bumpy."

Expanding on that last remark, the Ferrari boss pinpointed the most concerning part of the track, where he would most like to see action taken before FP3, after numerous cars were seen bottoming out over the bump heading into the first corner.

"Probably a bit too much before Turn 1," the Frenchman added. "It's almost dangerous. We will have to do something [before FP3].

"But overall, I think that it was a good start to the weekend, but still a long way to go."

title: Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson hit with double penalties for 'unacceptable' Mexico clash
excerpt:
Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson have both been hit with a one-place grid penalty for the Mexico City Grand Prix, and handed a penalty point apiece, following their needless clash in second practice.

Just 13 minutes into FP2, and on approach to the stadium complex at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, Verstappen opted to dive down the inside at Turn 12 on a driver who was his Red Bull team-mate for three races only recently, due to Isack Hadjar sustaining a wrist injury.

Lawson, though, held his ground in his Racing Bulls machinery and jostled with Verstappen through the slow Turn 13 before the Red Bull driver ran over the right edge of the Racing Bulls' front wing at Turn 14, depositing debris on the circuit which needed to be cleared by marshals.

Verstappen claimed that Lawson's move "wasn't smart" when addressing the media before heading to the stewards to account for his actions.

Ultimately, the stewards decided that the move was considered "unacceptable" following a warning given to the team managers earlier in the day - with both drivers being handed a one-place grid drop and one penalty point on their super licences.

"The Stewards heard from the driver of Car 3 (Max Verstappen), the driver of Car 30 (Liam Lawson), team representatives and reviewed video evidence," began the verdict.

"On the approach to turn 12 car 3 was on a preparation lap and car 30 was on a cool down lap preparing for another push lap. The drivers of both cars behaved in a manner that was considered unacceptable by the Stewards, particularly in view of the warning that had been given at the Team Managers meeting earlier this day.

"Both drivers admitted the moves were unnecessary and “clumsy”.

"Noting that there had been similar incidents this year of actions between drivers in Free Practice, the Stewards have decided to escalate the penalty from that of a formal warning to a grid position penalty, particularly in view of the warning that had been provided at the Team Managers meeting and consistent with other incidents involving contact between the cars in Free Practice in previous years.

"Competitors are reminded that they have the right to appeal certain decisions of the Stewards, in accordance with Article 15 of the FIA International Sporting Code and Chapter 5 of the FIA Judicial and Disciplinary Rules, within the applicable time limits."

title: Max Verstappen hits out at Liam Lawson: 'Not very smart behaviour'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has offered a cutting appraisal of his clash with Liam Lawson during FP2 at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Verstappen said it was "not very smart behaviour" for Lawson to "pick a fight" with him, given the precarious position the New Zealander finds himself in at Racing Bulls.

Despite enjoying a terrific season, the 24-year-old is in danger of losing his seat to Red Bull junior and F2 driver Nikola Tsolov.

A popular position within the F1 paddock is that Lawson has done more than enough to secure his future, but he could still find himself on the outside looking in, even though he is ninth in the drivers' standings as best of the rest and has carried the Faenza-based squad to the brink of fifth place in the constructors' championship.

Reflecting on the incident with Lawson, which has seen both called before the stewards, Verstappen issued a blunt account of the Racing Bulls driver's uncertain position.

"I was on a fast out lap because I had some little issues, so I was pushing on quite a bit," the four-time F1 drivers' champion said. "He was driving really slowly, so I was like, 'All right, let's go for it.'

"But as soon as he saw me arrive, he started to speed up... I don't know what was going through his head when that happened, trying to just run me off the track.

"For me, it's just not very smart behaviour when you're in his position to pick a fight with me."

Early in the second free practice session, the pair raced wheel-to-wheel through the tight, twisty and technical stadium complex at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodríguez when contact was made, damaging both cars.

The debris, which was strewn over the track, triggered a red flag stoppage. When the session resumed, Verstappen went on to go fifth fastest, with Lawson in ninth.

Asked whether the damage to his RB22 cost him during the remainder of the hour, the Dutchman continued his frank assessment of the situation.

"The bargeboard... was broken up," Verstappen added. "So of course you lose downforce for that."

title: Confusion over Colton Herta F1 status after strange mix-up
excerpt:
Colton Herta has not yet done enough to secure his FIA superlicence, after Cadillac erroneously claimed he was just one point away before his FP1 outing at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Taking part in the first free practice hour at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez was supposed to help the American reach the required threshold of 40 points, which is needed to race in F1.

This is because rookie stand-in drivers for those sessions earn a solitary superlicence point if they complete 100km. Herta therefore needed to complete 24 laps, and racked up 30.

However, it has now been established that a mistake on the IndyCar website incorrectly listed him as finishing sixth in the standings last year, when, in actuality, he finished seventh.

Therefore, he earned two fewer Super Licence points than the six that were originally thought. The FIA has confirmed that Herta remains on 39.

This highlights that Cadillac's maths was wrong when approached last week by RacingNews365, with the team insistent that he was on 39 points and one away heading to Mexico.

In reality, the nine-time IndyCar winner secured one point in 2023, 30 in 2024 when he finished second in the American championship, and four last year.

Those 35, coupled with the four he has earned for first free practice sessions for Cadillac in 2026 — in Barcelona, Austria, the United States, and now Mexico — bring the F2 driver to 39 of 40 required.

The good news for Herta is that he has multiple opportunities to secure the necessary points, with rounds in São Paulo and Las Vegas coming up on the F1 calendar before the schedule turns to either Qatar and Abu Dhabi or Imola.

The 26-year-old is believed to be in contention for Valtteri Bottas' seat alongside Sergio Perez for the 2027 season, despite his underwhelming performances in Formula 2.

title: Charles Leclerc sweeps Friday practice again as Lewis Hamilton suffers Ferrari woe
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc made it back-to-back Friday practice sweeps after finishing quickest in FP2 for the Mexico City Grand Prix.

A week ago, ahead of the United States Grand Prix at the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Leclerc topped both Friday sessions in his Ferrari, throwing himself into the running for a second win of the season, only to struggle in qualifying and finish second behind Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli in the race.

Seven days later, Leclerc again led the way on the timesheet at the end of first and second practice at the high-altitude Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, setting a leading soft-tyre run of one minute 17.827s.

In contrast, on the other side of the Ferrari garage, team-mate Lewis Hamilton lost over 30 minutes of running after being told to stop his SF-26 whilst on track after the seven-time F1 champion suffered a loss of power.

Behind Leclerc were McLaren's Lando Norris and Mercedes' George Russell, split by just three-thousandths of a second, and a tenth adrift of the Monégasque.

[Article continues below]

Following an FP1 in which 10 rookies took up seats to fulfil the regulations that guarantee them an outing during the season, the full complement of race drivers was on track for the second session.

The surprise at the start was a mix of tyres amongst the field, with Max Verstappen opting for a runout on the softs from the off. The seven-time F1 champion sat out FP1 for reserve Ayumu Iwasa.

It was Leclerc, though, who set the early benchmark, starting where he finished after topping the first session. The Monégasque posted a medium-tyre run of 1:18.257s.

Just 13 minutes in, however, it was Verstappen who was involved in an incident with Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson that sparked a red flag.

Approaching the stadium complex, Verstappen opted to dive down the inside at Turn 12 on a driver who was his team-mate for three races only recently, due to Isack Hadjar sustaining a wrist injury.

Lawson, though, held his ground and jostled with Verstappen through the slow Turn 13 before the Red Bull driver ran over the right edge of the Racing Bulls' front wing at Turn 14, depositing debris on the circuit which needed to be cleared by marshals.

After a five-minute delay, racing resumed with Leclerc spearheading a Ferrari one-two, with Hamilton three-tenths of a second adrift, only to then quickly drop behind Antonelli, albeit by just two-thousandths of a second.

On soft tyres, Norris edged ahead of Leclerc by 0.096s, a position the latter should have regained when he ventured out on the red-striped Pirellis, only to make a mistake on his first attempt into Turn 12, and another error into Turn 1 on his second try.

Soon after, Hamilton's session ended after declaring that "something's wrong with the power". The 41-year-old was forced to pull off track after Turn 4, sparking a VSC period as his car was wheeled back behind the barriers by marshals.

Switching to a fresh set of softs, Leclerc made no mistake on his third push lap, ousting Norris, who had improved to 1:17.930s, by just over a tenth, a position he maintained through to the finish.

Champion-in-waiting Antonelli was fourth quickest, two-tenths adrift, followed by Verstappen and Hadjar, three-tenths and four-tenths back respectively.

Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad and Lawson then sandwiched Alpine's Pierre Gasly in seventh and ninth, with McLaren's Oscar Piastri completing the top 10, albeit 0.642s off the pace.

Gabriel Bortoleto, who missed most of the session with a technical issue, propped up the timesheet in his Audi, 2.347s down.

title: Audi learn stewards' verdict after costly mistake hurts British rookie
excerpt:
Audi has been fined €7,500 for releasing Freddie Slater onto the track in an unsafe condition during FP1 at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Slater, taking part in his first official F1 session, was sent out at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez with a cooling fan still placed in the right-hand sidepod of his R26.

Whilst the team quickly realised the error, instructing the British driver to return to the garage, it caused his power unit to overheat, which appeared to have ended his session after just half an hour and zero push laps.

The stewards took a dim view of the mistake and handed down the fine to the team.

Thankfully for Slater, Audi was able to cool the car down adequately for him to head back out with a few minutes of the first free practice hour remaining, allowing the 18-year-old to set some timed laps.

He finished the session P21, going quicker than Colton Herta in the Cadillac, and will also take part in FP1 next week in Brazil.

According to the official FIA decision document, the stewards said: "Although the fan did not fall off the car (as was the case of a car in Australia this year), there was the possibility it could have.

"Accordingly, a penalty similar to that applied to Car 12 [Kimi Antonelli] in Australia was applied."

This resulted in the amount being mitigated down to the decided figure.

title: Red Bull provide power unit-at-altitude update after Isack Hadjar issues
excerpt:
Will the altitude shake up the F1 pecking order this weekend? Laurent Mekies suspects it just might.

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has confirmed Isack Hadjar's power unit issues in first practice for the Mexico City Grand Prix were not altitude-related, but has warned that compromises will have to be made over the remainder of the weekend.

Heading into this weekend, natural concerns were raised as to how the new-for-2026 PUs, with its near 50/50 split between combustion and electrical energy, would operate in the considerably thinner air of Mexico City's Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

Early in FP1, Hadjar encountered what was quickly diagnosed to be a PU problem. Although he later returned to the track, his programme appeared to then be muted as he finished 11th quickest, 1.417s behind pacesetter Charles Leclerc in his Ferrari, and unusually for a team driver, behind reserve Ayumu Iwasa by almost half a second.

Dismissing any concerns, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, Mekies said: "There have been no unfortunate issues so far related to the altitude.

"In fairness, we did have a PU issue with Isack and lost a bit of track time, but the guys did a very good job and managed to send him back on track. But nothing linked with altitude.

"It's still a long weekend. I hope it's definitely fixed."

[Article continues below]

Mekies predicts 'one-off race' with 'compromises'

Due to the conditions, however, Mekies knows that all 11 teams on the grid will have to compensate to various degrees to complete Sunday's race.

The Frenchman feels the field could be given an unusual shake-up depending on which team manages to overcome the conditions the most successfully.

"In many respects, everybody will not be operating at their optimum this weekend," said Mekies. "PU side for the altitude, chassis side for the temperature, and we are all ready to make some compromise to make sure our car can survive, and our PU can survive in these conditions.

"Then, where does that compromise put us in terms of relative competitiveness? It'ss not something we can assess in FP1, but it's something that will become apparent as the other sessions develop.

"I think we all expect that this race could be a one-off in terms of the picking order. We don't really have an idea whether we will have an advantage or a deficit this weekend. Only time will tell.

"But what is sure is that there is a fair amount of lap time, PU side plus chassis side, that is unusually in the game this weekend, so let's see how it pans out."

title: Ultra-rare Ayrton Senna 1994 F1 Williams set for multi-million pound auction
excerpt:
A 1994 Williams F1 car driven by Ayrton Senna is to be auctioned next month - one of just two surviving FW16s the Brazilian drove.

FW16 chassis 01 was driven by Senna during pre-season testing and during the morning warm-up ahead of the 1994 Brazilian GP before he reverted to a different chassis for the race.

Senna was killed during the third race of the season, at the San Marino Grand Prix, driving chassis 02, which was later returned to Williams, and is believed to have been destroyed.

Chassis 01 was gifted to the Senna family at the end of 1994 as per a clause in Senna's contract which stated he was to be gifted an example of the FW16 if the team won the constructors' championship title - which it did after beating Benetton.

After Senna's death, FW16 chassis 01 was used as the spare car for Damon Hill in Monaco, before David Coulthard made his debut in the chassis at the Spanish GP in Barcelona.

The chassis was then used by Nigel Mansell during his comeback at the French GP, and was also driven by Coulthard in the British GP before it became a test machine or was used as the spare car, including for Hill in Japan and the title-deciding Australian GP.

The machine is to be auctioned next month in New York by RM Sotheby's, with an estimate of £2.950 million GBP to £4.450 million.
